name: Wellington
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Wellington: public sector and regulatory matters, appellate litigation support and due diligence in NZ.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Wellington: dealings with central government and its agencies, regulatory inquiries by bodies based in the capital, litigation that reaches the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, and due diligence on suppliers and partners in the region. Scoped from Nashville with qualified New Zealand professionals.
intro: Wellington is New Zealand's capital and the seat of Parliament, the Cabinet, most government departments and many Crown entities and regulators. The Wellington region had an estimated 543,400 residents in June 2025, according to Statistics New Zealand subnational estimates, and the Wellington urban area about 209,800. The regional economy is dominated by services, which contributed about three quarters of regional GDP in the year to March 2018, and regional GDP per capita has been among the highest in the country. Public administration, professional services, finance and insurance, information technology and the screen and creative industries are prominent. CentrePort, majority owned by Greater Wellington Regional Council, runs the harbour port and the Cook Strait ferry terminals that link the North and South Islands.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Wellington because so many decisions affecting business in New Zealand are made there. Suppliers and consultants bidding for government contracts, firms subject to inquiries by regulators based in the capital, and parties in appeals heard by the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court all generate research needs. Typical engagements include due diligence on government suppliers and their principals, background research for counsel in regulatory and appellate matters, reviews of conflicts of interest and lobbying relationships, and checks on technology and professional services firms concentrated in the city. Port and ferry logistics through Wellington Harbour also feature in supply chain and freight inquiries.

matters.title: Government supplier due diligence
matters.text: Ownership, directorship, litigation and media history of firms and principals supplying central government agencies in Wellington, built from Companies Office records, published judgments and open sources, to support procurement decisions, subcontractor vetting and partner selection for public sector bids.

matters.title: Regulatory inquiry support
matters.text: Fact development and background research for counsel acting for organisations facing inquiries or enforcement by regulators headquartered or active in the capital, including research into complainants, former employees and counterparties, scoped so that findings fit the regulatory process and privilege strategy.

matters.title: Appellate and Supreme Court matters
matters.text: Targeted research for counsel in appeals before the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, both of which sit in Wellington, where new evidence is tightly controlled; work usually focuses on enforcement readiness, related proceedings and counterparties rather than reopening facts.

matters.title: Conflicts and influence mapping
matters.text: Lawful mapping of relationships between companies, advisers, lobbyists and former officials connected to policy or procurement decisions in Wellington, drawing on public registers, published disclosures and media, to support board governance reviews, bid protests and internal investigations.

matters.title: Technology and creative sector checks
matters.text: Background research on Wellington technology, software and screen-industry companies, their founders and investors before investment, licensing or co-production arrangements, covering corporate history, related parties, intellectual property disputes, insolvencies and reputational issues in New Zealand and overseas.

local_context.title: Senior courts in Wellington
local_context.text: Wellington is home to New Zealand's senior appellate courts. The Supreme Court sits at 85 Lambton Quay, and the Court of Appeal, the principal intermediate appellate court, sits permanently in Wellington, hearing civil and criminal appeals from the High Court and certain second appeals with leave. Most appeals end in the Court of Appeal rather than the Supreme Court. The High Court and District Court also sit in Wellington for first-instance commercial and civil matters.

local_context.title: Regulators in the capital
local_context.text: Many national regulators and Crown entities are based in Wellington alongside the ministries they report to, including the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, which runs the Companies Office. The Financial Markets Authority and Commerce Commission also have a significant Wellington presence. Inquiries by these bodies, and documents they publish, are often central to investigative work touching the city.

local_context.title: Registries and local records
local_context.text: New Zealand company, director and shareholder information is held nationally by the Companies Office and searchable online, so there is no separate Wellington registry. Property-related information such as rating and consent records is held by the relevant territorial authority, such as Wellington City Council or Hutt City Council, and requested through each council's own processes. Title searches are usually carried out through New Zealand counsel.

local_context.title: Port, ferries and regional trade
local_context.text: CentrePort Wellington manages the main port in Wellington Harbour, handling containers, logs, vehicles and bulk cargo, and leases wharves to the Interislander and Bluebridge Cook Strait ferries. Greater Wellington Regional Council holds a 77 percent shareholding. The port is a link in North and South Island freight flows, which makes it relevant to cargo theft, freight fraud and supply chain inquiries.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Wellington, TDSC starts by identifying the decision-maker involved: a government agency, a regulator, an appellate court or a commercial counterparty. That shapes the timetable, the records available and how findings will be used. Research relies on Companies Office records, published judgments, agency publications, Official Information Act releases obtained by the client or published by others, and open sources, handled under the Privacy Act 2020. TDSC does not seek non-public government information and does not approach officials on a client's behalf. Where interviews or field inquiries are needed, TDSC coordinates private investigators licensed under New Zealand law and works with the client's counsel. TDSC has no office in Wellington.

faqs.q: Can TDSC vet a supplier before a New Zealand government contract?
faqs.a: Yes. TDSC reviews ownership, directors, related companies, litigation, insolvency history and media coverage of suppliers and subcontractors, focusing on issues that matter to public sector buyers such as conflicts of interest and prior contract disputes. Findings support the client's decision and are not legal advice or a substitute for the agency's own procurement checks.

faqs.q: Does TDSC help with appeals in the Court of Appeal or Supreme Court?
faqs.a: Yes, as a consultant to counsel. Because new evidence on appeal is tightly controlled, TDSC usually supports appellate matters by researching related proceedings, counterparties and assets relevant to enforcement once a judgment is final. The work is documented so its sources can be checked. Counsel decides what, if anything, is put before the court.

faqs.q: Will TDSC obtain information from government agencies in Wellington?
faqs.a: TDSC works only from lawful sources. It does not seek confidential government information or approach officials to obtain it. Where official information may be relevant, the client or its counsel can make requests through the proper statutory channels, and TDSC can help analyse published or released material alongside other records.

faqs.q: Can TDSC map lobbying or influence relationships in Wellington?
faqs.a: TDSC can map publicly documented relationships between companies, advisers, former officials and decision-makers using company records, published disclosures, register entries and media. The work is factual and source-based. It does not involve surveillance of officials or politicians, and conclusions are presented with the limits of the public record stated.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office or investigators in Wellington?
faqs.a: No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Wellington or elsewhere in New Zealand. Engagements are run from Nashville. Where a matter needs local inquiries, TDSC coordinates independent investigators holding the licence required under New Zealand law and works with the client's New Zealand counsel within an agreed written scope.
